steps.say: A cinema trip. No algebra, just compare the two orders.
steps.hint: The only difference between the two orders is one extra ticket, and £7 of price.

steps.say: That move, comparing the orders so the popcorn cancels, is called elimination. You just subtracted two equations without noticing.
steps.hint: One ticket (£7) and a popcorn cost £12 together.

steps.say: Using a value you know to find the one you do not is substitution. Those two moves are the whole topic. Algebra just writes ticket as \(x\) and popcorn as \(y\): \(2x + y = 19\) and \(x + y = 12\).

steps: Elimination: multiply to match coefficients, then add/subtract
Or Substitution: rearrange one equation and substitute
Solve for one variable, then back-substitute for the other
method_card.title: How to Solve Linear Simultaneous Equations
method_card.content:
Elimination: Make the coefficients of one variable equal, then add or subtract to eliminate it.

Substitution: Rearrange one equation for one variable, then substitute into the other.

Always check your answer in both original equations.

steps: Sometimes no single multiplication works. Multiply BOTH equations to hit a common target: \(3y\) and \(2y\) both become \(6y\) with \(\times 2\) and \(\times 3\).
Everything else is the same: same signs subtract, opposite signs add, substitute back, check.
Prefer rearranging? Substitution also works: make \(y\) the subject of one equation and put it into the other. Either method earns full marks.
gold.title: Gold: multiply both equations

steps: You need the one pair of values, an \(x\) AND a \(y\), that fits both equations. In bronze a matching pair is already there (like \(+y\) in both).
Same Signs Subtract: subtract one equation from the other, right-hand sides too, and the matched letter vanishes. Opposite signs (\(+y\) and \(-y\))? Add instead.
Solve the one-letter equation that is left, then substitute back into the easier equation to find the other letter.
bronze.title: Bronze: the pair already matches

steps.label: Match
steps.content: Both have \(+y\), the same sign, so subtract.

steps: Now nothing matches yet. Multiply ONE whole equation, every term and both sides, until a pair matches.
Then it is a bronze question: same signs subtract, opposite signs add.
Substitute back and check your pair in both equations.
